name: Hrádecký dub

location.address: Beside the Hrádecký mill pond (Hrádecký mlýnský rybník), Hrádek u Sušice, Klatovy District, Plzeň Region
location.neighbourhood: Hrádek u Sušice, about 4km from Sušice

access: Free, open public ground on the bank of the mill pond; no gate or ticket
transport: In Hrádek u Sušice village, about 4km from Sušice; no public transport reaches the pond directly, reachable on foot or by road from the village
story:
This oak was a sapling while the Thirty Years' War was tearing through Bohemia. Czech Wikipedia puts it at about 440 years old; a Czech tourism site says nearer 400. Neither says how the number was reached, so read it as a range rather than a birthday, but either end of it lands the tree's first years before 1648.

What is not in doubt is the size. It stands 28 metres tall with a crown twenty metres wide, on the bank of the mill pond at Hrádek, four kilometres outside Sušice. It has been a protected memorial tree since 1978, and the tourism site, last updated in 2021, calls it a truly massive tree in good condition.

The trunk is over four metres round, though exactly how far over depends on whom you ask. The Czech memorial-tree register's figure is 411 centimetres; Wikipedia quotes 485 from a 2012 measurement under the same register number. They cannot both describe the same day's measurement, and if you have a tape and a spare minute at chest height, we would like to know which is closer.

There is no legend attached and no famous visitor on record. What there is, is a pedunculate oak that has stood over the same water for four centuries, through wars and a working pond's ordinary seasons, and it still carries a full crown. Czech Wikipedia names two more protected limes nearby, the Hrádecká lípa and the Lešišovská lípa, which we have not yet checked ourselves.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its size: a pedunculate oak 28 metres tall, with a trunk over four metres round and a crown about twenty metres wide. It stands on the bank of the Hrádek mill pond.

name: Buk u rybníčku

location.address: By a former pond on the edge of the village, Nová Ves pod Pleší, Příbram District, Central Bohemian Region
location.neighbourhood: Nová Ves pod Pleší, about 9km from Dobříš

access: Free, on open ground by a pond at the edge of the village; no gate or ticket found in any source
transport: Nová Ves pod Pleší village, Příbram District; about 9km from Dobříš, roughly 40km southwest of Prague; no direct public transport to the pond itself
story:
Birds nest in this beech, and a fungus is eating it, and both facts are in the official record. When Czech conservationists inspected the tree in 2019 they noted a large branch torn away and a big open wound, rot, tinder fungus fruiting at the base of the crown, and a smaller cavity in use as a nest. Fifteen years earlier, in 2004, the same record had found one open cavity and a crown only five percent dead. It is a veteran in the full sense of the word: old enough to be falling apart, and still doing it slowly.

It stands by a former pond on the edge of Nová Ves pod Pleší, roughly forty kilometres southwest of Prague, which is where the name comes from: Buk u rybníčku, the beech by the little pond. The state declared it a memorial tree in September 2004. A regional heritage site counts it as one of the village's two memorial trees and says stories have already grown up around it, without telling us which.

The trunk is 308 centimetres round. That is modest for a lone park beech and respectable for one that grew up with neighbours competing for light, which is what this one is.

Nobody has published an age for it, and we are not going to invent one. If you know the village's stories, or when the pond was drained, we would like to hear them.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the storm wound where a large branch tore off in 2019, and the tinder fungus at the base of the crown. It is a beech, 308 centimetres round, by the old pond outside the village.

best_time.label: October, when the beech turns copper and russet
